entries.headline: New York in 3D: Manhattan's streets and towers on Earth
entries.text: Come down over New York, within a few tens of kilometres of Manhattan and under 30 km up, open the layers button at the top right and switch on New York (3D city). Slop New York, a 3D model of Manhattan's buildings, streets, parks and piers, builds in a few seconds and stands at its place on the globe, lit by the same Sun at the simulation's time and hazed by the same air. It stays off until you switch it on, since it's a big download (about 140 MB), and a link you share keeps it on. Its lights don't show at night yet.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: All of Starlink joins the satellites, with a search, and you choose which to see
entries.text: All 11,116 Starlink satellites can now show round Earth, with a slider for how many, the first by serial number, from one to all; and Iridium's 80 in their polar planes. In Earth's panel, the Satellites section has a search that finds Earth's satellites alone, a switch for each kind (Starlink, Iridium, navigation, weather, the space stations...) and a slider for how many names to show. The names hold still as the satellites move, those behind Earth no longer crowd out those in front, and selecting one keeps its one name. A link keeps what you chose.

entries.headline: The slow way to the Moon, by way of the Sun
entries.text: The Earth's and the Moon's Craft sections now have a ballistic lunar transfer: the low-energy route NASA's GRAIL and CAPSTONE took. The craft goes out about four times the Moon's distance, where the Sun's pull bends its orbit round, and falls back three to four months later to meet the Moon almost at rest, needing far less fuel to stop there than a direct flight. Switch it on and the app flies the first one leaving from the clock's date, drawn with the craft where it is on that day.

entries.headline: The James Webb Space Telescope, where it really is
entries.text: Webb is now in the sky beside the Earth, drawn with NASA's own 3D model at its real size and lit by the Sun, its sunshield turned toward it. It follows JPL's record of its path, from 41 minutes after launch on Christmas Day 2021, out to its orbit around the Sun–Earth L2 point 1.5 million km beyond the Earth, and on along its planned path to October 2031. Search for "JWST" to fly there, zoom in to a few metres and orbit it; from behind its sunshield it eclipses the Sun. Outside those dates it isn't shown.

entries.headline: The Moon's frozen orbits: the few low orbits that last
entries.text: With the Moon selected, the orbits spacecraft use near it are drawn around it. Low lunar orbit is a thin shell. The four "frozen" inclinations, 27°, 50°, 76° and 86°, are where the pulls of the Moon's lumpy mass concentrations average out, so an orbit lasts for years. Also drawn are the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter's two orbits and a 30-hour elliptical frozen orbit that hangs over the south pole. The info panel explains why most low lunar orbits crash within weeks or months.

entries.headline: Fly a spacecraft to the Moon
entries.text: The Earth's and the Moon's panels now have a Craft section: switch on transfer to the Moon and a spacecraft leaves a low orbit round the Earth that day, burns once, and coasts four and a half days to pass 100 km over the Moon. Its path is drawn with the craft where it is at the clock's time, and the panel gives its burn, how long it takes and what it would cost to stop at the Moon. Behind it is a new flight simulator: the craft is pulled by the Earth, the Moon and the Sun where the app draws them, and it flies a real spacecraft, NASA's TESS, to within a few hundred metres of where it really went.

entries.headline: The tubes that lead on and off halo orbits
entries.text: Switch on a halo or Lyapunov orbit around a Lagrange point, then its Manifolds, and you see the paths a spacecraft can drift along onto that orbit (green) or off it (red) without firing its engines. Together they form tubes that reach from the orbit toward the planet or moon at either end. Low-energy missions to the Moon and to the Sun–Earth Lagrange points follow these tubes. This works for every pair of bodies; around the Moon, Gateway's orbit gets none, because it is almost stable.

entries.headline: Satellites round Earth: the ISS, GPS, the geostationary ring
entries.text: Near Earth, with the orbits on, about 450 real satellites now circle it where they are on the date: the space stations, Hubble, every navigation satellite, weather satellites, the Molniya satellites on their long northern loops and a sample of the geostationary ring. Search for one ("ISS", "Tiangong", "Hubble", a NORAD number) to target it and see its orbit and how old its elements are, then go to it to ride along 300 km away.

entries.headline: Settings and About open without the page blinking
entries.text: Opening Settings or About, bottom left, used to blank the whole page for a moment before the dialog appeared, and closing it did the same. The dialogs now open and close over the scene with no blink.

entries.headline: A tidier info panel, and a sheet you can pull up on your phone
entries.text: The panel beside a planet, moon or star now starts with its name, what it is and how far out it orbits, then the few numbers you'd ask first: its size, its day, its year. Everything else (its orbit's elements, its mass and gravity, the space around it, its atmosphere) waits in sections you open when you want them, and nothing in the scene shows through. On a phone the panel is a sheet at the bottom of the screen: pull it up for more, push it down to see the sky. Cesium's credits shrink to its logo a few seconds after Earth's close-up surface comes into view (tap the logo to read them), and leave the screen while you look up at the sky.

entries.headline: Halo orbits, Gateway's NRHO and the spirographs of three-body space
entries.text: The orbits spacecraft fly around Lagrange points can now be drawn. Open a planet's or moon's info panel, and under space around switch on its halo, Lyapunov and distant retrograde orbits, or around the Moon the near-rectilinear halo orbit that NASA's Gateway station is planned for. They are drawn moving with the pair of bodies, where their shapes make sense, or fixed in space, where they trace the spirograph loops seen from Earth. Where NASA/JPL's catalogue of these orbits covers the pair (the Earth and Moon, the Sun and Earth or Mars, Phobos, Europa, Titan), the orbits drawn are JPL's own.

entries.headline: Earth's orbital neighbourhoods: LEO, GPS, Molniya and the edge of cislunar space
entries.text: With Earth selected, the regions satellites use are drawn around it: low and medium Earth orbit as faint shells, GPS's six orbital planes, the long Molniya and Tundra loops over the north, the graveyard just above the geostationary ring, and a sun-synchronous orbit that rides the line between day and night as the Earth goes round the Sun. Further out, outlines mark where the Moon's pull starts to matter and where cislunar space ends. Mars shows its own sun-synchronous orbit.

entries.headline: Lagrange points, Hill spheres and stationary orbits around every planet and moon
entries.text: Pick a planet or moon and the points where a spacecraft can hold station with it show up around it: its five Lagrange points with the body it orbits (JWST's Sun–Earth L2, the Moon's L1 and L2), the edge of the space its gravity rules, and the orbit that keeps pace with its turning, like Earth's geostationary ring. They follow the real orbits as they move. The info panel's new space around list gives their distances, and says why the Moon, Mercury and Venus can't have a stationary orbit.

entries.headline: Earth's night side stays dark while its terrain loads
entries.text: Close to Earth, until the detailed terrain arrives (or for good, when it can't load), Earth's night side used to show the daytime surface, dimly, under the city lights, and the city lights looked dimmer for it. The night side is now dark there, as it is once the terrain is in. This is the first fix we make to Cesium, the engine behind Earth's close-up surface, in our own copy of it, and we're offering it to Cesium's authors too.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: See an orbit's six elements on the orbit itself
entries.text: A body's info panel now lists its orbit's six elements as they are right now: its size and shape, the tilt and turn of its plane, where it comes closest, and where it is along the way. Click any of them to light them on the orbit in space, drawn as the textbooks draw it: the two planes, the line where they cross, each angle an arc with an arrow. They stay on as you go to other planets and moons, so you can compare how Earth's and Venus's orbits line up, and a link keeps them and the panel as you left it. The orbit drawn is the one the body is on at that moment, so it meets the body however close you zoom. The guide's orbit page works again, and the panel's masses and units are fixed.

entries.headline: What's new shows the highlights, and filters by features and fixes
entries.text: What's new on the homepage now opens on the featured updates: the changes most worth a look, each with its view. A filter bar above the list has "Featured only", which you can turn off for every update, and "Features" and "Fixes", which you can turn on and off to find one or the other; the count beside it follows. celestiary remembers your choice. When a featured update has been announced on X or Facebook, small icons beside its links open the post. The "new" count counts the featured updates, and the changelog tour follows the filter.

epic.title: What's new: a changelog, in the app, and as posts

entries.headline: The stars arrive first and faster: the naked-eye sky in a tenth of the download
entries.text: The star catalogue, 107,000 stars, was the biggest thing the first screen waited for: one 1.8 MB download. Now the sky you can see with the naked eye, about 8,900 stars and every star with a name, comes first in 157 KB, and the rest stream in once the scene is showing, the part of the sky you are looking at first, fading in over a couple of seconds rather than popping on. The homepage's first screen downloads 925 KB instead of 2.6 MB. Names, search, picking, star labels and the constellations work from the start, a link to a faint star opens as soon as its part of the catalogue is in, and the sky looks the same once it is. Gaia's stars fade in the same way as you fly among them.

entries.headline: Flights from the homepage start where you can see them
entries.text: Choosing a scene on the homepage, a search result there or a What's new entry now fades the homepage away first, with the scene behind it holding still, and only then sets off. When the scene is at a different date, the date changes during the trip, at a moment when nothing on screen would show it, so the trip runs without going dark. The flight begins gently over a second and a half, so you can see which way you're going, before the fast part of the trip and the arrival.

entries.headline: The first screen loads faster: the rest waits until you need it
entries.text: Celestiary used to download the place names of 24 worlds, 175 galaxies and this changelog before showing anything, and the planets and moons as 31 separate files. Now the planets and moons come in one file, a world's place names when you fly close to it or open a link to one of its places, the galaxies when you search, follow a link to one or look deep enough for one to show, and the changelog when you open What's new. The homepage makes 30 requests instead of 86, and nothing looks different.

entries.headline: Earth loads faster: each picture is downloaded once
entries.text: Opening Earth, or a link to it, used to download the month's 4096-pixel Blue Marble map three times, once each for the surface, the clouds and the close-up layer, and the 1.4 MB backup cloud picture came with every view though the day's satellite clouds replace it. Now the map is downloaded once and shared, and the backup picture is fetched only where the satellites saw nothing, mostly the polar night, and then as a 128 KB copy. Earth looks the same.

entries.headline: The first screen loads faster: the planets' tables come after it
entries.text: Celestiary now loads about 2.6 MB less before the first screen: the tables that place the planets were most of the app's code, and they now load right after the scene appears. The code on the first load is 668 KB compressed instead of 2 MB. For the second or two until they are in, the planets are drawn from approximate orbits, within a quarter of a degree of where they should be, and then glide to their exact places over a second and a half, so nothing jumps.

entries.headline: Celestiary has its own address: celestiary.org
entries.text: Celestiary now lives at celestiary.org. Links to the old celestiary.github.io address, including links to a scene, keep working: they go to the same place at the new one.

epic.title: What's new: a changelog, in the app, and as posts

entries.headline: Earth's clouds without a seam at the date line
entries.text: Earth's daily clouds no longer show a hard vertical edge across the Pacific at 180°. The day's cloud map was cut there between satellite passes a day apart, so the clouds on each side didn't match. The 20° east of the date line now blend into the clouds from the day before, which were seen at the same time as the other side of the cut. The map still appears as soon as the day has loaded, and the blend follows a moment later.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: What's new on the homepage, and a tour of it
entries.text: The homepage has a What's new button that opens the latest changes, each with its date and a few words on what you can now see or do. An entry with a view flies there as the homepage's cards do, and a small count on the button shows what has come since your last visit. A tour plays the entries that have a view one after another, a caption under each: start it from the panel, or open #;news:tour at the site's address. Space pauses it, the arrow keys skip, Esc stops it, and it cuts between views instead of flying when your device asks for less motion.

epic.title: What's new: a changelog, in the app, and as posts

entries.headline: The homepage tour flies into Earth's shadow to see the city lights
entries.text: The homepage's tour now passes over the evening's edge of daylight into Earth's shadow, where the Sun is hidden behind Earth and the air glows as a thin ring round it. It waits there while your eyes adjust, and the city lights come up. It picks whichever lit-up region is near midnight when you visit: Europe, India, East Asia or the Americas, or the nearest lit coast when midnight is over the Pacific. While the page loads, a little Moon now turns through its phases under the title.

entries.headline: Earth's clouds without a seam down the Atlantic
entries.text: Earth's daily clouds no longer show a hard edge along 36° W. Each day's cloud map now appears all at once when it has loaded, and a day the satellites haven't finished covering waits for the latest complete one, so neighbouring pieces of the map always come from the same day.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: A homepage at celestiary's address
entries.text: Open celestiary with nothing after the address and you get a homepage: the title, a search box and four scene cards over a slow tour of the live scene. The cards are tonight's sky from where you are, Earth at dusk, the Moon hiding Jupiter and Gaia's stars, and each flies to its view. Esc or a click on the scene leaves the homepage, and Back returns to it.

image.alt: The homepage's Earth card: dusk reaching South America

entries.headline: A calmer first load, and overlays that fade
entries.text: The page opens in your light or dark theme and dims to black, then brings in the title, the scene, and the orbits, labels and controls one after another. Orbits, labels, grids and the controls now fade in and out when you toggle them. A link that hides the controls loads with no text at all.

entries.headline: Stars drawn as the eye sees a point of light
entries.text: A bright star now has a white core and a halo that grow with its light, by the published function for how the eye scatters light. Sirius is about 9 px wide on a 1080 px screen, and a star ten times brighter is about twice as wide. Raising the star limit with ] no longer turns every bright star into the same disc, and the Sun's glare is now drawn from any distance.

entries.headline: The Sun has sunspots, a corona and eclipses
entries.text: The Sun now follows the date: sunspots from the observed record (1997 to today, then the forecast), prominences and flares, a corona that changes with the cycle, and the solar wind. When the Moon covers it you get a total eclipse. The link is Dallas at mid-totality on 8 April 2024.

epic.title: Stars up close: a dynamic Sun, and every star from its physical parameters

entries.headline: Clouds you can fly into
entries.text: From about 30 km down, Earth's flat cloud layer gives way to ray-marched clouds with depth, seeded from the day's NASA satellite picture and tallest where the clouds are thickest. The link looks straight down from 12 km over the Gulf of Mexico on 28 August 2005, the day before Hurricane Katrina's landfall.

epic.title: Distinctive appearances: Sun, gas giants, rings, auroras

entries.headline: A million of Gaia's stars
entries.text: Gaia's brightest stars, down to magnitude 10.8, are in: 925,686 added to the bundled Hipparcos catalogue. They load in tiles as you look, brightest first, and move with the date. About a hundred naked-eye stars the old catalogue left out now show too.

epic.title: Milky Way: realistic structure, a million Gaia stars, and galactic dynamics

image.alt: Gaia's stars and the Milky Way from 3,200 light-years out

entries.headline: 175 galaxies you can fly to
entries.text: SPARC's 175 disc galaxies are drawn from their published size, distance, tilt and rotation, on the same light model as the Milky Way. Search one by name and fly there. A galaxy's panel plots its rotation curve against the one its visible matter would give.

epic.title: Deep-sky objects: nebulae, galaxies, Sgr A*

entries.headline: Place names on 23 bodies, and labels that no longer pile up
entries.text: Mercury, Venus, the Moon, Mars, 18 moons and Pluto now carry names from the IAU Gazetteer, 8,226 places in all, the largest shown first as you come closer. A label that would touch a more important one now steps aside, so Jupiter and the Galileans read "Jupiter" and "Callisto", not five names on top of each other.

entries.headline: Planets arrive at the right brightness
entries.text: Going to Mars or Jupiter right after loading (4, then g) used to arrive dark and take a few seconds to brighten. The exposure now follows where you are going, so a body arrives at its settled brightness, and a far body hands over from its dot to its disc without a jump.

entries.headline: `f` makes the camera follow a body along its orbit
entries.text: Press f and the camera rides a body's orbit as time runs, so the planet stays put on screen while you look around. It turns on when you go to a body, and the link keeps it, so a shared view reloads still following. The link is Jupiter, followed, with time running at 16,384x.

entries.headline: Right skies on the giants, Titan and Triton
entries.text: The skies of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Titan, Pluto and Triton were dimmed twice for their distance from the Sun, and looked too dark. They now follow the sunlight they get, and Saturn's rings are lit on their own scale. The link is Titan's sky from 10,000 km.

entries.headline: Sunlight falls off as the inverse square
entries.text: Planets at different distances now keep their true brightness against each other in one frame. Before, the outer planets were too bright next to Earth, Neptune by almost five stops.

entries.headline: The Moon lit and shaped like the real Moon
entries.text: Both Moons, celestiary's own and Cesium's, now share one lunar brightness law: the full Moon is flat to the limb, and a crescent is no longer about three stops too bright. Crater walls catch the low Sun along the terminator, from LRO's elevation map, and the dark side shows earthshine. The link is the Moon hiding Jupiter, seen from Ohio.

image.alt: Jupiter and its moons slipping behind the Moon's limb

entries.headline: Stars show at a telescope's field of view
entries.text: At a narrow field, no star could show at any exposure. A star now keeps its size on screen as you zoom in, so the faint star beside Jupiter in the occultation view shows once you raise the exposure about eight stops with =.

entries.headline: Earth's detailed imagery loads only up close
entries.text: Bing imagery on Earth is requested only when you are low enough to see it, so the Cesium account's monthly quota lasts. From higher up, Earth shows NASA's Blue Marble. The night side is also no longer lit on the bare ellipsoid when Cesium's terrain is refused.

entries.headline: Steering at a telescope's field
entries.text: Dragging and the pitch keys now turn the view by the same number of screen pixels at every field of view. At a telescope's 0.07 degrees, one pixel of drag used to swing the scene by about 1,650 pixels.

entries.headline: Jupiter is smooth at a telescope's field
entries.text: Seen from Earth's ground at a telescope's field, Jupiter was a disc of black holes and stray pixels, because the atmosphere pass drew the wrong body's air. It is a smooth disc now.

entries.headline: A shared link holds more of your view
entries.text: A link now holds the clock (paused, or a rate such as 8x), the stars' setting, tracking and the exact field of view, so a view reloads as it was shared. A star you picked with Look at is the link's target. The link looks at HIP 46635 from Ohio with the clock paused and the star limit raised.

entries.headline: Exposure keys, and tracking that keeps your roll
entries.text: Press - and = to make the picture darker or brighter by a third of a stop, and e to reset it; the link keeps it as ev=. Tracking with t no longer squares the camera to the ecliptic, so your roll holds while the target stays centred. The time keys j, k and l now work while paused.

entries.headline: Faster near the ground, and a `?perf=1` panel
entries.text: The Cesium layers skip work they cannot show (the Moon behind Earth, the night lights by day), the exposure meter reads the screen without stalling it, and the atmosphere over the ground is cheaper. Add ?perf=1 to the address for a panel of GPU and CPU time per pass. The link is the ground view used to measure it.

entries.headline: Fixed: a flat blue disc when looking toward the Sun
entries.text: Looking toward the Sun from above Earth's day side, with Earth behind you, a flat saturated blue disc used to appear where the atmosphere pass found a hit behind the camera. It is gone.

entries.headline: Mars's aureole round the Sun
entries.text: The bright ring of dust-scattered light round the Sun on Mars was 3.5 times too wide and 9 times too faint at its core. It now has the width and brightness of 1.5 micron dust. The link faces the Sun from Valles Marineris.

entries.headline: The Milky Way's band at night, from inside
entries.text: From a dark site the band of the Milky Way now shows at the dark-adapted eye's sensitivity, where the night sky used to be black. It comes from a model of how the eye pools faint light over large areas.

entries.headline: The Milky Way from a published structural model
entries.text: The galaxy is now its stars' combined light, drawn from published models: the bar at 27 degrees, four arms as Reid and colleagues measured them, dust lanes, the warp, thin and thick discs, and a boxy bulge. From outside, it frames itself like a photograph. The link looks at it from about 150,000 light-years out.

epic.title: Milky Way: realistic structure, a million Gaia stars, and galactic dynamics

entries.headline: Every star drawn from its own temperature
entries.text: The Sun's surface is drawn from physics (granulation, spots, bright faculae, limb darkening), and every catalogue star uses the same renderer with its own temperature, radius, rotation and activity. Published values are used where they exist, and estimates from the catalogue where they do not.

epic.title: Stars up close: a dynamic Sun, and every star from its physical parameters

entries.headline: Earth has real clouds again
entries.text: Earth's clouds come from NASA's daily satellite picture for the simulation date, back to the year 2000, drawn as one shell over both celestiary's Earth and Cesium's. Change the date and the weather changes. The link is the Gulf of Mexico on 28 August 2005, the day before Katrina's landfall.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: One target, shown everywhere
entries.text: What you click, search for or travel to is now the one target, and the breadcrumb, the link and the tracking key all agree on it: Sun, Earth, New York. Reload a link and the same thing is targeted.

entries.headline: Fixed: Earth ran out of memory at a telescope's field
entries.text: Zoomed far in from Earth's ground, Cesium asked for ever finer terrain tiles on distant ground and the page ran out of memory. Tile detail is now bounded at narrow fields. The link is the view that crashed.

entries.headline: City lights on Cesium's Earth
entries.text: Cesium's Earth now has city lights on its night side, from NASA's Black Marble, at the same scale as celestiary's own. The link is Europe at night from 4,000 km.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: The star guide works again
entries.text: The /guide/star page was broken: its star links went to the app root, and the star was a white disc. Its links now stay on the page and the star is drawn.

epic.title: Stars up close: a dynamic Sun, and every star from its physical parameters

entries.headline: Place names show over Cesium's globes
entries.text: Names on Earth, the Moon and Mars had gone missing whenever Cesium's layer was on. They show again, and search finds a place under its body. The link is Earth from 12,000 km with the names on.

entries.headline: Fixed: white dashes over distant planets
entries.text: From Earth's ground at a telescope's field, white concentric dashes used to cover Jupiter's disc. The atmosphere pass no longer draws air over them.

entries.headline: Fixed: far stars vanishing on Apple GPUs
entries.text: On Apple GPUs, stars more than 1,950 light-years from the camera turned black, Alnilam in Orion among them. They draw at any distance now.

entries.headline: The debug axes are gone from the Sun and planets
entries.text: The axes that showed through at extreme zooms and near the camera's clip plane are no longer drawn.

entries.headline: Triton, Janus and Rhea at their real sizes
entries.text: Triton was ten times too small, Janus ten times too large and Rhea twice too large. Their radii now follow JPL's values.

entries.headline: Exposure that adapts like the eye
entries.text: Stars, the Milky Way and the Sun's disc are now in physical units, and the exposure is metered from what is on screen. The day sky hides the stars by its light, twilight and night bring them out, Mars's low-Sun sky comes up, and the Sun's granulation shows. The exposure eases over about a second. The link is the Australian outback at civil twilight.

entries.headline: Every body turns by the IAU's rotation model
entries.text: Every body but Earth now turns by the IAU's pole and prime meridian, within 0.003 degrees of JPL Horizons. Before, every body except Earth and the Moon turned once a day from an arbitrary meridian. Moons that keep one face to their planet now do.

entries.headline: Double-click or double-tap a label to go there
entries.text: On a phone there is no g key. A double click or double tap on a planet's, moon's or star's label now goes to it, the same way the search's Go button does.

entries.headline: The scene fits phones and the dock
entries.text: The scene no longer runs under the widgets dock, and it resizes when a phone turns or its browser bars come and go. The drawer opens as a sheet on a phone, and touch no longer floods the console with errors.

entries.headline: Search: Go and Look at
entries.text: The search bar has two actions. Go (the arrow, or Enter) travels to the result. Look at (the magnifier) targets it and turns the camera to face it without moving, for checking which face of a body points at you. Narrowing the field of view now draws the body you look at.

entries.headline: The widgets drawer and its apps are in the link
entries.text: A link now restores the drawer (open or closed, docked, which app is showing, which are pinned or running) and each app's settings. The link has the Human expansion app open on a 6-neighbour spread, halfway along.

entries.headline: Human expansion: spread across the stars
entries.text: A what-if app: humans leave the Sun at half the speed of light and spread from star to star across the catalogue, drawn as one line per hop. At the defaults every star is reached in 50 hops and about 46,000 years. It is the first app in a new widgets drawer and dock, which can pin and stop apps, and asterisms and orbits are now drawn as smooth wide lines.

entries.headline: Mars's day sky
entries.text: Mars's sky from the ground was nearly black away from the Sun and white toward it. Multiple scattering, for every body, and Mars's dust as published give it a sky of scattered light all round. The link looks up from Valles Marineris.

entries.headline: Standing below a body's datum
entries.text: You can now stand below a body's reference surface, in Valles Marineris on Mars or at the Dead Sea on Earth, and see a sky, a horizon and terrain without the black bands and flicker that were there. The link is Valles Marineris, 232 m up, the Sun low.

entries.headline: Orbit drag slows as you near the ground
entries.text: Orbit drag (Option+drag, or the orbit mode that auto picks beyond about three radii) used to sweep 32 km of Earth per pixel at 5 km up. It now slows with altitude, so you can move a few kilometres over the ground.

entries.headline: One HDR pipeline for all the light
entries.text: Light is now drawn in physical units into one linear buffer and tone-mapped once, so the sky, Cesium's Earth and celestiary's own bodies are brightened by the same law. Earth's Cesium layer sits under celestiary's atmosphere, which hazes Cesium's terrain for its own distance.

entries.headline: Moons show as dots from afar, and hide behind planets
entries.text: A moon's far point was a dim grey dot, drawn in the wrong colour space and lost among the stars, and it drew on top of its planet. Moons now show as dots from far away, and a nearer planet's disc hides them.

entries.headline: Orbit lines lie on the bodies' real paths
entries.text: Orbit lines are drawn from the same ephemeris that places each body, so the dots sit on their lines. Before, each line was a flat ellipse centred on the primary, with no tilt, and fast clock rates left lines that never finished rebuilding. The clock now stops at the dates the ephemerides hold, 6,000 years either side of 2000.

entries.headline: Pluto and the moons in their real orbital planes
entries.text: Pluto and every moon but ours now move on published mean elements, in their real orbital planes, checked against JPL Horizons. The planets with moons, and Pluto, tilt to their IAU poles, so the moons' planes and Saturn's rings agree with the drawn equators.

entries.headline: Stars and planets in one frame
entries.text: The planets and the Moon were placed in the ecliptic of the date and the stars in J2000, 0.37 degrees apart in 2026. Stars, constellations and the Milky Way now shift with the date as well, so the whole scene is in one frame.

entries.headline: The Moon on a real lunar theory
entries.text: The Moon's position now comes from Meeus's truncated ELP-2000/82 lunar theory, within a few arcseconds of JPL Horizons over 1950 to 2050, in place of a fixed ellipse that was far off. Its rotation and orbit periods read 27.32 days, not about a year.

entries.headline: Landing on Cesium's terrain, not in it
entries.text: On Earth, the Moon and Mars the ground under the camera is now the floor. Zoom no longer carries you into mountains that rise kilometres above the sphere (Everest, Olympus Mons), and landing with another body targeted no longer clips Cesium's sky into a black edge.

entries.headline: Earth in the month's Blue Marble
entries.text: Earth is NASA's Blue Marble for the month of the simulation date, drawn the same by celestiary and by Cesium, with high-resolution detail coming in close to the ground. Arriving at Earth and Mars is smoother. The link is Earth from 20,000 km.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: Cesium's Moon and Mars swap in smoothly, lit like celestiary's
entries.text: A body's Cesium layer starts loading when you target it or one of its moons, and crossfades in once its tiles are ready. The exposure follows the target, so Mars and Earth no longer arrive blown out. The Moon uses LRO's WAC mosaic, and far planets show again as points. The link is the Moon at quarter phase from 5,000 km.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: Mars's sky is no longer washed out
entries.text: The dust scattering formula had a factor wrong, which made Mars's sky near white from the surface. It is fixed. Stars show through Cesium's sky, far views lose their speckles, Venus has its colour back, labels draw over haze, airless moons lose their rim, and v hides Cesium's credits.

entries.headline: Cesium is the default, with celestiary's sky over Mars
entries.text: Cesium's globes are the default for Earth, the Moon and Mars, drawn for every one in range. Cesium has no atmosphere for Mars, so celestiary's own is drawn over it, and a moon in front of its planet, Phobos over Mars, keeps its depth so the haze stops at it. The link is Mars from 12,000 km.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: A Cesium data view of Earth, the Moon and Mars
entries.text: Near Earth, the Moon or Mars a Layers button appears. It switches between celestiary's own globe and Cesium's, with real terrain and imagery; the Moon and Mars need a Cesium ion token. If Cesium's terrain cannot load, Earth falls back to Natural Earth imagery rather than empty space. The link is the Ganges plain from 7.5 km.

epic.title: Earth appearance parity across the Cesium swap

entries.headline: Place names wait until you zoom in
entries.text: On a 4K screen every named city showed at the first fly-in. Only the biggest names show from afar now, and finer ones come in as you close in.

entries.headline: Double-click anywhere to land
entries.text: Double-click or double-tap any point on a body's surface to drop a latitude and longitude marker and land there, not only at named places. Stars are left out, so you do not land on one by accident.

entries.headline: A sky view for your phone
entries.text: Hold your phone up at night and the planets, stars and constellations line up with the real sky, from the phone's orientation sensors (iOS Safari and Chrome on Android). On a desktop it shows what the view would be. Land on Mars and look up, and you see Mars's sky.

entries.headline: Earth, the galaxy and the grids in their true orientation
entries.text: Three linked bugs are fixed: the Milky Way's disc now lies in the same plane as the Hipparcos stars, Earth's rotation is right, and the equatorial, ecliptic and galactic grids are in their real frames. Sirius lands where its catalogue position says.

entries.headline: Stars from the ground at night
entries.text: Stars show from a planet's surface at night and through deep twilight, while the day sky stays an opaque blue. From space the lit hemisphere shows its terrain through the haze.

entries.headline: Places, click-to-land and city lights
entries.text: Named places (cities, craters, landing sites) appear on Earth, the Moon, Mars, Mercury and Venus as you come closer. Click one, or search for it, to fly in and land on the surface. Earth's night side has city lights from NASA's Black Marble, and the latitude and longitude in a link now match the surface you see. The link goes to New York.

entries.headline: Drag orbits a planet from far, looks around from close
entries.text: Dragging now orbits a body when you are looking at it from afar, and looks around when you are close to the surface. A drag-mode setting (auto, pan or orbit) overrides it, which also fixes phones, which have no Alt key.

entries.headline: Fixed: dragging on a phone
entries.text: Dragging to rotate did nothing on mobile. Touch, pen and mouse now all work, and a drag keeps tracking past the edge of the canvas.

entries.headline: Reference grids, a first Milky Way, and settings in the link
entries.text: Equatorial, ecliptic and galactic grids, each switchable, with labels that slide along the screen edge. A barred-spiral Milky Way, with the Sun on one arm. Constellations, labels, orbits, grids and the controls travel in the link as s=, and Shift+V hides all annotations.

entries.headline: Search from the breadcrumb
entries.text: The search bar sits in the breadcrumb and searches the part of the sky you are in: named stars and any Hipparcos number. Highlighting a result previews it in the info panel.

entries.headline: Click a star to travel to it
entries.text: Click a star in the field and fly there. The camera keeps its place through the jump, which ends the glitch of arriving to look at empty space, and stars stay steady at any distance.

entries.headline: Saturn's rings, lit and shadowed
entries.text: Saturn's rings have a shader of their own: ice glints, rings that brighten when backlit, and Saturn's shadow falling across them, with the rings' shadow on Saturn.

epic.title: Distinctive appearances: Sun, gas giants, rings, auroras

entries.headline: Shareable links to any view
entries.text: The address now holds the whole view: the target, the date, the camera's place and direction, and the field of view. It updates a second after the camera settles, and pasting it in a new tab restores the view nearly pixel for pixel. The link is Mars.

entries.headline: Atmospheres from precomputed scattering
entries.text: Skies and planetary limbs now use Bruneton's precomputed scattering instead of a ray-march per pixel, so there are no stepping artifacts. The link is Earth from 20,000 km.

entries.headline: Fly the camera like a spaceship
entries.text: The arrow keys pitch and roll the camera, dragging looks around, and Option+drag orbits a planet. Zoom approaches a surface smoothly and never clips through it, and going to a body flies there in about a second and a half with no jump.

entries.headline: Star names and constellations on by default
entries.text: Star labels and constellation lines are on when you open celestiary, the starting camera is set farther back, and the planet-name toggle works.

entries.headline: The planets on VSOP87
entries.text: The major planets are placed with the VSOP87 theory. The simulation clock shows the date more clearly, and pausing it works properly.
